title: CryoNet.Refine: One-Step Diffusion for Structure Refinement
one_liner: A diffusion model learns to nudge atomic coordinates into experimental density maps, automating and speeding up protein structure refinement.
lead: Cryo-electron microscopy measures fuzzy 3D pictures of molecules, and scientists must fit detailed atomic models into these blurry maps. This is tedious work, requiring weeks of hand-tuning and expensive software. CryoNet.Refine automates it: a neural network learns to adjust atomic positions intelligently in one forward pass, replacing manual labor with a trained model that handles proteins, DNA, RNA, and their complexes.

problem.h2: Why structure refinement is a bottleneck
paras: Cryo-EM machines capture electron-density maps (3D images showing where atoms are likely to be) but these images are grainy and low-resolution. A researcher must manually move atomic coordinates to fit the map, improving the alignment and chemical realism. This refinement step matters deeply but is slow: existing software like Phenix and Rosetta demand weeks of computation and careful hand-tuning of many numbers (settings like learning rates, iteration counts, and weighting factors).

A naive approach: randomly tweak coordinates and see if the fit improves. This works but is glacially slow, because the space of possible structures is enormous and random guessing almost never finds the right direction to move.

callout.html: Current refinement software is slow, demands manual tuning, and cannot handle diverse biomolecule types consistently.

steps.text: Take the rough atomic model and the experimental density map together.
Convert atom positions and the map into lists of numbers the network can process.
Neural network guesses how far to move each atom toward better alignment, because it has learned from thousands of examples which atom motions raise the density correlation.
Ensure moved atoms stay chemically valid: correct bond lengths, angles, and chirality.
Return the adjusted coordinates, ready to use.

paras: The paper changes how atomic coordinates are nudged. Instead of expensive iterative optimization software tweaking positions over many steps, a single forward pass through a trained neural network outputs the refined coordinates directly.

hidden.name: model-to-map correlation
paras: This is a numerical score (ranging from 0 to 1) measuring how well a proposed set of atomic coordinates matches the experimental electron density. A score near 1 means the atoms align beautifully with the fuzzy map; near 0 means mismatch. The traditional refinement software maximizes this score by trial and error.

CryoNet.Refine estimates this hidden score during training: the neural network learns to predict which moves will raise the correlation most. By teaching the network patterns from many examples, it learns to make smart moves in a single step, rather than slowly grinding through iterations like traditional software.

heat.caption: Darker atoms have higher correlation with the density map. Stars mark atoms the model targets for adjustment.

reads.html: The correlation score is simply how much the fuzzy density map agrees with where you placed the atoms.
Model-to-map correlation is computed as the overlap integral between the atomic model and the experimental electron density, normalized by map variance.

mechanism.h2: Why moving coordinates in one step works
paras: A diffusion model is a neural network trained by watching examples: given a randomly-scrambled atomic structure and its target density map, the network learns to guess a small correction. By training on thousands of real refinement problems, it absorbs patterns: bonds should stay the right length, atoms should move toward high-density regions, and chirality (left- vs. right-handedness of molecules) must be preserved.

When you run the finished network, you start with a rough model and the experimental map. The network runs once and outputs a delta: how much to adjust each atom. A density-aware loss encourages changes that boost alignment, because moves that better fit the fuzzy map earn a lower loss score during training. Stereochemical restraints act as guardrails, blocking moves that break chemistry: atoms pushed violently out of valid positions get heavily penalized. The result is a single fast pass replacing hours of optimization.

This works because the network has seen enough real examples to internalize two hard problems at once: (1) where the density is high (atoms belong there), and (2) what valid chemistry looks like (bonds and angles). It distills this knowledge into one forward pass.

stages.s: Rough atomic coordinates and experimental density map
Encode both as lists of numbers

math.words: Total loss equals the negative correlation between model and map, plus a penalty for moving atoms that violate chemical rules.
math.equation: Loss = -correlation(model, map) + lambda * sum_i (L_bond_i + L_angle_i + L_chiral_i)
symbols: how well atom positions overlap with the fuzzy density
weight controlling how strictly to enforce chemistry
penalty if bond length strays from the normal range
penalty if a three-atom angle strays from normal
penalty if an atom's handedness flips

worked.title: A toy example
lines: After one step: correlation improves to 0.85, so first term is -0.85
But move breaks two bonds slightly: L_bond total = 0.2, L_angle total = 0.1, L_chiral = 0
Final loss = -0.85 + 0.15 = -0.70 (negative because we want high correlation)
The network learns: maximize correlation, but never at the cost of breaking chemistry.

math.note: The network is trained to maximize correlation while respecting chemical validity, encoded as a single loss combining alignment and stereoconstraints.

bars.h2: Comparison: old workflow vs. this paper

charts.title: CryoNet.Refine (one-step diffusion)
charts.note: Fast because it is a single forward pass (no iteration), automated because the network has learned to find good moves (eliminating manual testing), and achieves comparable alignment because the training loss directly rewards matching the density map.

items.html: If the network was trained only on soluble proteins but you apply it to membrane proteins (which have different chemistry), it may struggle because the training examples did not cover that case.
If the starting atomic coordinates are so far from the truth that the network cannot recognize the structure, one step is not enough. The network assumes the input is already a reasonable guess.
In low-resolution maps or regions with flexible loops, multiple coordinate sets may fit equally well. The network picks one, but the wrong one might win by chance if the map is very noisy.
When starting with a decent rough model and applying the model to structures similar to its training data, CryoNet.Refine converges fast and reliably.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small refinement test: take a known protein structure, blur it into a synthetic electron-density map, intentionally misalign the atomic coordinates (shift them by 0.5 Angstroms), feed both into CryoNet.Refine, and measure the correlation before and after. Run the same experiment on 10 different proteins. Report the median correlation improvement and the time taken.
demo.closing: The demo should make it obvious that one neural-network pass recovers most or all of the correlation that traditional software would find over hours, and it does so in under 1 second.
